claims.text: A tailored heat treatment can induce coherent nanoscale precipitates in a predominantly single-phase high-entropy alloy matrix.
Formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates will synergistically improve strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The proposed starting material is a near-single-phase, chemically homogeneous, coarse-grained high-entropy alloy with minimal secondary phases.
Solution treatment followed by optimized aging can nucleate and grow uniformly distributed coherent nanoscale precipitates while avoiding deleterious segregation.
The effect requires an alloy composition capable of precipitating an intermetallic phase coherent with the matrix.
Suitable diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving force are required for nanoscale precipitate formation.
Over-aging or precipitate coarsening can prevent the combined mechanical-property improvements.
Significant chemical inhomogeneity or incoherent precipitates may cause embrittlement and eliminate the expected benefits.
The treatment will produce a hierarchical microstructure containing uniformly distributed coherent nanoscale precipitates and possibly submicron grain refinement.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and increase strength through precipitation hardening.
Coherent precipitate–matrix interfaces reduce stress concentrations.
Reduced stress concentrations and effective load transfer from coherent precipitates enhance ductility.
Microstructural refinement increases Young's modulus.
The refined precipitate-containing microstructure improves fracture resistance through crack deflection and energy absorption.
The tailored treatment is expected to increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional processing.
The tailored treatment is expected to increase strain to failure.
The tailored treatment is expected to produce a modest increase in Young's modulus.
The tailored treatment is expected to improve fracture toughness.
Conventionally processed comparison samples have coarser microstructures and inferior combinations of mechanical properties.
Excessive precipitate density or precipitate size can reduce ductility and fracture resistance.
